`npksum()` evaluates kernel-weighted sums that can be combined into custom
estimators and test statistics without dropping immediately into C.

## Why `npksum` matters

Use it when the required object is not already exposed by a higher-level
estimator.

In practice, it can be used to:

- build custom kernel estimators,
- form weighted kernel sums,
- experiment with leave-one-out constructions,
- prototype new statistics and test objects.

## A simple local-constant example

A concise illustration recovers the local-constant conditional-mean estimator

$$
\widehat g(x)=
\frac{\sum_i K_h(x-X_i)Y_i}{\sum_i K_h(x-X_i)}
$$

from two kernel sums.

```r
## Recover a local-constant fit directly from the underlying kernel sums
library(np)
data(cps71, package = "np")

fit_lc <- npksum(txdat = cps71$age,
  tydat = cps71$logwage,
  bws = 2)$ksum / npksum(txdat = cps71$age,
  bws = 2)$ksum

plot(cps71$age, cps71$logwage, xlab = "Age", ylab = "log(wage)", cex = 0.1)
lines(cps71$age, fit_lc, col = "blue")
```

The numerator is a response-weighted kernel sum; the denominator normalizes the
weights at each evaluation point.

Numeric `bws` input is materialized against the supplied data before dispatch.
This matters for custom mixed-data calculations: continuous, unordered, and
ordered columns retain their data-aware kernel types rather than being treated
as a default all-continuous bandwidth object.

## What to keep in mind

`npksum()` supplies kernel sums rather than a complete estimator. A custom
construction should therefore:

- check your variable classes,
- check your bandwidth choices,
- verify the object you are constructing really corresponds to the statistic you intend,
- validate on small known cases first.

## When should I use `npksum`?

Use it when:

- you are prototyping a custom estimator or test,
- you need direct access to weighted kernel sums,
- you want to expose the mechanics of a standard kernel estimator.

For standard estimation, prefer higher-level functions such as `npreg()`,
`npudens()`, `npcdens()`, and `npqreg()`.
